slides.transcript: Module one. Rack geometry, datums, and alignment. MGX version one point two builds on Open Rack version three, adding shared mechanical, power, and liquid interfaces for accelerated computing. We'll trace the alignment chain from the rack frame to the tray and cartridge. We'll examine the dimensions, supports, and reference surfaces that make a common interface usable. The goal is to connect an apparent fit with the engineering evidence that demonstrates compatibility.

slides.title: Six engineering reviews, one interface system
slides.subtitle: Follow requirements from geometry to acceptance evidence.

slides.transcript:
This course is organized as six engineering reviews. We start with rack geometry and alignment, because every connection depends on a controlled physical position. Then we examine tray and board envelopes, followed by modular input and output bays. The fourth review covers busbar electrical design and grounding. The fifth follows liquid interfaces and blind-mate mechanics. The final review connects load cases, qualification, and acceptance evidence.

We'll use the MGX version one point two contribution as a design reference. You'll distinguish a shared interface from an example implementation, and a published condition from an assumption in your own product. Familiarity with rack infrastructure, direct current power, cooling loops, and engineering drawings is assumed. Keep one question in mind throughout: which source requirement and which implementation evidence support this compatibility claim?

slides.title: Start with the requirement and its reference
slides.subtitle: Table 1 applies unless a dimension has a separately specified tolerance.
slides.transcript:
A compatibility review starts by locating the requirement, its reference, and its applicability. MGX version one point two defines common rack and tray interfaces for power, liquid, mounting, and retention. It also defines space and mounting for tray-to-tray interconnects. It does not prescribe every connector or the electrical architecture of every fabric. Power shelves, top-of-rack and management switches, cooling distribution units, and input and output or power cabling design are outside this contribution's scope.

The power rack reference design presented by Jared Huntington at the twenty twenty-six OCP Global Summit supplies useful system context. Its eight-hundred-volt distribution link and power converters sit around the rack and tray interfaces reviewed here. We will keep that implementation example distinct from the requirements of this contribution.

The version boundary matters. The specification describes one point two as derived from, but not fully compatible with, MGX one point one. A familiar family name is therefore not evidence that an earlier part is interchangeable.

A datum is the reference used to establish a feature's location or orientation. Blind mating means the interfaces engage without direct manual access to the mating connection. That makes the complete reference chain important, rather than just the nominal position of one connector.

Table one gives default tolerance categories. Hole center to hole center is plus or minus zero point one two seven millimeters. Hole center to edge is plus or minus zero point two five four. Edge to edge returns to zero point one two seven. Feature size is plus or minus zero point one zero zero millimeters. Board thickness is plus or minus ten percent of nominal.

For a hole-to-edge check, use the hole-to-edge category unless the actual dimension specifies something else. Record the controlling drawing and any separately specified tolerance before combining dimensions into an illustrative stack-up.

slides.title: Build around the mating interfaces

slides.transcript:
The rack additions are easiest to understand as a sequence of interface needs. Begin with the Open Rack version three base structure. MGX adapts it to support nineteen-inch E I A equipment on a one-rack-unit pitch. The front region also provides space for input and output cabling, management connectivity, latching, and slide components. That space serves a mechanical and service purpose as well as a wiring purpose.

The rear extender is an optional addition that increases rack depth to twelve hundred millimeters. It protects rear components such as cable bracing and manifold fittings, while maintaining the existing rear hole pattern for doors or seismic bracing as needed. A drawing that includes the extender should not turn this optional feature into a universal requirement.

The supports and stiffeners establish locations for the rack manifolds and interconnect cartridge. The manifolds provide the rack-side liquid connections. The cartridge region provides a controlled volume and mounting structure for a selected interconnect implementation.

The rack supports an I T payload up to four thousand pounds. That is a rack-level capacity statement. It does not establish the rating of an individual slide, bracket, or connector support. Each of those still needs evidence for its actual use.

Treat the developing assembly as a reference chain: base structure, mounting features, supports, mating interfaces, and the installed tray. When a proposed component changes one link, review the affected dimensions and loads. The engineering question is which interfaces remain controlled after the change, and what evidence demonstrates that control.

slides.title: Carry the datum through the manifold support

bullets.text: Read manifold positions from Figures 12–14.
Use the released bracket drawings for critical-to-function features.
Connect mounting position to the tray's mating location.

slides.transcript:
A manifold connection can be correctly dimensioned relative to its bracket and still miss the tray if the bracket's rack reference is wrong. The review must carry the datum through the entire support chain. Start with the rack references, locate the mounting features, identify the bracket's controlling dimensions, and then locate the manifold-side interface.

Figures twelve through fourteen give rack manifold locations, base geometry, and mounting detail. The accompanying two-dimensional drawing package provides the detailed bracket and assembly features. The contribution specifically directs implementers to those drawings for critical-to-function dimensions and tolerances. Three-dimensional geometry supplies additional details, but a nominal model does not replace a separately specified tolerance.

For an engineering exercise, trace one selected tray-side liquid connection back through the rack manifold support. Record which feature establishes position at each step. Classify a selected hole-to-edge dimension using Table one, unless its drawing states a different tolerance. Keep the coordinate direction visible; a signed offset is not interchangeable with an unsigned distance.

This exercise produces a review map, not a complete tolerance analysis. Your product may require an additional stack-up involving bracket manufacture, mounting clearances, rail location, and connector float. Those assumptions must be explicit and checked against the actual drawings and supplier interfaces.

The result should let another engineer answer three concrete questions: which reference locates this mating feature, which requirement controls that location, and which inspection or assembly evidence shows that the manufactured system meets it?

slides.title: The slide is part of the connection system

bullets.text: T-pin positions are referenced to chassis Datum A.
Slide features support and align the tray to rear interfaces.
The latching surface enables interoperable latch designs.
Verify the selected supplier's tray-weight capacity.

figure.alt: Specified T-pin locations and blind-mate rail feature details.
figure.caption: Common rail geometry supports a repeatable alignment chain; capacity remains supplier specific.

text_inventory.review_record: Final native images / encoded states and transition frames visually reviewed; OCR used as transcription assistance.

slides.transcript:
The slide rail does more than carry the tray during service. It is part of the mechanism that positions the tray for interconnect and liquid engagement. A change to the slide interface can therefore affect both mechanical support and rear mating alignment.

The contribution establishes preferred T-pin locations referenced from chassis Datum A. Using those locations enables a common slide rail interface across the ecosystem. A variance requires a unique rail design, even when the tray's outside dimensions look familiar.

The blind-mate slide features support and align the tray to the interconnect cartridge and the rack manifolds. The specified latching surface enables latch designs for blind-mate liquid implementations and interoperability between the slide and chassis. Treat the rail, T-pins, chassis, latch, and rear interfaces as related features. Checking each part in isolation misses the relationship that establishes the final position.

Capacity is a separate question. The specification directs the implementer to ensure that the particular supplier implementation safely supports the weight of the compute or switch tray being installed. The rack's overall payload figure cannot be substituted for this rail-level evidence.

During a substitution review, retain the chassis reference, compare T-pin positions and geometry, verify the alignment and latching features, and obtain the relevant load capacity. Document which features are common and which depend on the selected supplier. A standard mounting pattern reduces unnecessary variation, but it doesn't remove the need to validate the complete supported and engaged assembly.

bullets.text: Stiffeners reposition in 1RU increments.
Front-to-back stiffeners are 2U high.
Cross-rack stiffeners are recommended above and below the cartridge.
27RU and 36RU cartridge drawings are example implementations.

figure.caption: Support placement follows the cartridge geometry and loading of the selected implementation.

slides.transcript:
Rack reinforcement is configurable because interconnect implementations do not all impose the same geometry or load. The cross-rack and front-to-back stiffeners can shift in one-rack-unit increments. Front-to-back stiffeners are two rack units high. Their spacing depends on the particular implementation and its loading requirements.

The contribution recommends cross-rack stiffeners in the spaces above and below the interconnect cartridge. These provide stiffness, mounting, and alignment features for the cartridge support brackets. Additional stiffeners, or closer spacing, may be appropriate for larger cartridges or higher loads. That is an implementation decision that needs evidence.

The twenty-seven and thirty-six-rack-unit cartridge drawings are examples. They illustrate mounting and alignment locations and a recommended datum and tolerancing scheme. The specific connectors, guide pins, and electrical architecture are not prescribed, because those depend on the accelerator and system design.

Separate two review steps. First, establish the cartridge volume and mounting geometry. Then review the loads that act through the connectors and supports. We'll examine the documented force cases in the final module. Here, the task is to keep the structural context connected to the interface locations.

If a design changes cartridge height, connector population, support spacing, or bracket arrangement, don't carry over an earlier structural conclusion without checking its applicability. Record the selected example or implementation, its reference geometry, and the evidence for support placement. Configurability creates useful options, but each chosen configuration still requires a coherent alignment and load path.

slides.transcript:
The mechanical review connects requirements that are easy to separate accidentally. Begin with contribution scope and the revision boundary. Then identify the actual datum and tolerance that control each selected feature.

The nineteen-inch adaptation, optional extender, manifold supports, and cartridge structure serve different interface needs. Carry their relationships into the manufactured assembly. The rail and latch belong in the same alignment review as the rear connections. Their nominal locations and their supplier-specific capacities are different kinds of evidence.

Finally, connect stiffener placement to a defined cartridge implementation. Example mounting geometry is useful, but it is not a universal support rating. You should now be able to trace one tray-to-manifold reference chain and explain which drawing or requirement controls each step. That map becomes the starting point for reviewing a changed tray, rail, or support.

slides.transcript: Module two. Tray architecture, board envelopes, and DC-SCM. The common tray outline is only the beginning of a compatibility review. We'll compare hybrid and fanless cooling arrangements, examine full-width and micro MGX board constraints, and review the management-module interface. The aim is to identify the geometry, mounting, and electrical assumptions that remain controlled when you change an internal assembly. Keep the complete chassis reference and the actual board implementation in the same review.

slides.transcript:
By the end of this module, you'll be able to distinguish a shared outer chassis envelope from the mounting details inside it. You'll compare the dual-host-processor-module and full-size fanless examples, then trace their different liquid and input and output arrangements.

You'll read the board outline, mounting-hole rules, ground-pad boundaries, and component-height zones for micro and full-width MGX. You'll also account for the supporting pan and mechanical structures that aren't included in a simple board-component height limit.

Finally, you'll review the MGX datacenter secure control module. Its vertical one-rack-unit implementation uses a familiar connector-based interface, but implements a specified subset of the electrical pinout. The engineering objective is to identify what a proposed substitution changes, and which mechanical or electrical constraints must be verified before it can be accepted.

slides.title: A shared outside envelope can hide different interiors

bullets.text: Compute and switch trays use the MGX 1RU reference chassis.
Fanless uses the same outer dimensions with different mounting details.
Fanless tray cooling is 100% liquid; fans are not supported.

figure.alt: Hybrid compute tray and fanless dual-HPM example from the MGX specification.

slides.transcript:
A tray substitution must preserve more than the outside dimensions. The contribution defines a compute tray as a one-rack-unit chassis containing a central or graphics processing element. A switch tray contains the switching devices and interconnects for a multi-node network. Both use the MGX reference chassis.

The fanless compute tray uses the same outer chassis dimensions as that reference, but it does not retain all the same mounting-feature details. That distinction is explicit. Don't infer internal interchangeability solely from a shared width, height, and depth.

In the hybrid example, component placement includes an air-cooling fan zone and liquid-cooled processing regions. A host processor module, abbreviated HPM, is the processor-board assembly whose envelope and interfaces are controlled as part of the system.

The fanless tray performs one hundred percent of its tray cooling through the liquid loop. Fans are no longer needed or supported in this design. The removed fan zone creates opportunities for larger modules, integrated liquid distribution, and blind-mate input and output arrangements.

Those opportunities do not mandate one population. The contribution shows implementation examples, and their mounting features must be read in that context. During review, separate the common outer chassis boundary from the actual mounting, cooling, and connection features of your assembly. Ask whether the changed module preserves those interfaces, and whether its liquid-cooling implementation meets the conditions relevant to the complete tray. The rack-level heat-capture measure will be examined separately later in the course.

slides.transcript:
The fanless examples show two ways to integrate the same broad functions. The first has two host processor modules and an integrated cooling and input and output zone. That zone replaces the fan region. Its manifold and midplane assembly distribute liquid through blind-mate MQD connections and distribute input and output or management signals between modules and host processor modules.

The full-size example makes different choices. The chassis features used for rear installation of two micro MGX assemblies are removed, allowing the full-size module to install on MGX T-pin locations. The bay modules connect through coplanar connections rather than the separate midplane arrangement. Liquid distribution is integrated into the host processor module itself.

The supplied three-dimensional assembly gives a useful view of that integration. Separating its geometry reveals the board context, cooling structures, manifold, and connector regions. The separation is an instructional exploded view, not an approved disassembly sequence or a statement about operating joints. The source geometry is preserved; the display positions are intentionally expanded.

Use the comparison to identify interface ownership. In the dual-module example, a discrete manifold and midplane assembly carries important distribution functions. In the full-size example, some of those functions sit within the larger module. The location of a function determines which assembly changes when a different module is selected.

Before accepting a configuration, identify the actual chassis mounting details, bay interfaces, and liquid-distribution arrangement. Common family terminology does not make the two internal implementations identical.

slides.transcript:
Micro MGX is the half-width board family, allowing two assemblies within a nineteen-inch tray. Its outline and mounting holes follow the D C M H S D N O Type two definition identified in the contribution. Read the MGX figures for the actual dimensions and their applicable constraints.

Begin with the board outline and required mounting holes. Additional holes may be introduced for mechanical stability when the implementation needs them. Any fastener or mounting method contacting the board must remain within the specified ground-pad diameter. Adding a hole does not remove that contact boundary.

A keepout is a controlled region in which geometry or component height is restricted. The primary-side height options differ for memory-module-based and non-memory-module layouts. The contributed micro MGX C A D uses the non-memory-module option.

The other shown option illustrates an implementation choice; it isn't evidence that the supplied model contains both layouts. Secondary-side component-height limits do not include every supporting mechanical structure. Board pans, stiffening plates, and other added parts require their own keep-in or keepout consideration.

Some predefined areas require zero height to preserve the referenced modular-board compatibility. The micro board's secondary-side constraints assume a supporting pan within the overall assembly. Your pan may vary, but the completed geometry must still fit the controlled chassis relationship.

For a review exercise, mark the required mounting contacts and height zones, then list the mechanical structures added after board processing. That separates the printed-circuit-board component envelope from the complete supported module envelope.

slides.title: Include the pan and the mechanical stack

slides.transcript:
The full-width MGX board uses the available motherboard zone to provide a larger board envelope. It carries its own outline, required mounting locations, and maximum-height definitions. Do not derive those features by simply doubling the micro board dimensions. Use the full-width drawings.

As with the micro family, additional mounting holes may be introduced when needed. Mounting contact must remain within the designated ground-pad diameter. That rule keeps the fastening method connected to the intended mechanical and electrical contact region. Primary-side height options are shown for memory-module and non-memory-module layouts.

On the secondary side, the published component-height restrictions exclude supporting structures that may be required by the motherboard assembly. If a design adds a subpan or stiffener, it must add the necessary keep-in or keepout constraints for that hardware. Predefined zero-height regions still apply.

The supporting board pan is part of the overall assembly assumption used by the secondary-side height constraints. Review that pan together with board thickness, component height, mounting contact, and chassis location.

A board that meets a component-height figure can still produce an incompatible assembly if an added mechanical part occupies an uncontrolled region. For a substitution review, compare the primary and secondary zones separately. Identify the selected layout option and the mechanical structures added after board processing.

Then connect the finished module back to the tray mounting reference. The acceptance claim should describe the completed assembly, rather than only the bare board or one component population.

slides.transcript:
The MGX datacenter secure control module, or DC-SCM, adapts management-module integration to a one-rack-unit chassis. It installs vertically and uses an interface based on S F F T A one zero zero two. The board connector and support bracket are part of the mechanical relationship shown in the contribution.

The electrical review is separate from the shape check. The module implements a subset of the DC-SCI pinout. Table two provides the MGX one-rack-unit assignments. It includes defined power and ground contacts, management-related signals, and entries explicitly marked as not connected. A familiar connector family does not prove that an arbitrary module uses the same subset or signal assignment.

Use the pin table directly. Read the contact designation, the signal name, and the applicable implementation. Preserve distinctions such as power, ground, reset, clock, data, and not-connected entries. Don't silently replace the contributed table with a complete pinout from another module form factor.

A practical review has two linked records. The mechanical record identifies the board outline, vertical placement, bracket, and connector mating geometry. The electrical record compares the actual module and host assignments against Table two and the referenced interface requirements.

If a proposed module changes either record, document the effect. The contribution establishes a particular compact integration, not blanket interchangeability among every secure-control-module shape. The right conclusion is a source-supported statement about this module, its mating host, and the implemented interface.

slides.transcript:
The tray and board review separates common boundaries from internal choices. Hybrid and fanless examples use a shared outer envelope, but their mounting and cooling arrangements differ. The dual-module and full-size fanless designs place liquid and input and output distribution in different assemblies.

For both board families, read the actual outline and mounting figures. Keep board contact inside the specified ground pads. Identify the selected primary-side height option, preserve secondary-side zero-height regions, and account for the pan or stiffener that forms part of the completed assembly.

The compact DC-SCM adds an electrical boundary to its mechanical one. Compare the supported pin assignments rather than relying on connector familiarity. You should now be able to list the geometry, mounting, cooling, and electrical evidence needed for a proposed internal module change. That evidence is the foundation for selecting compatible front bay assemblies next.

slides.transcript:
By the end of this module, you'll be able to read a bay name as a location statement rather than a product label. You'll identify the rows and chassis positions consumed by a wide or taller bay, then compare that allocation with the actual chassis layout.

You'll distinguish the required widths of Types A through E from their example contents. You'll apply the short and long depth rule in the correct direction, including the separate CRPS optimized option for Type C.

You'll then connect the module envelope to its retention features. Spring and camming mechanisms use specified datum relationships, and a protrusion beyond the datum surface remains a system-design responsibility. Finally, you'll review the fanless Type B and E connection and enclosure dimensions. Those specific interfaces need their own check, even when a bay width matches a hybrid implementation.

slides.transcript:
The naming scheme makes a bay's allocation explicit. Every system is described with four bay locations across its width, in both the front and rear. Chassis height is described by rows, with each row representing one rack unit. The bay name combines row location, short or long depth, chassis position, and bay type.

A wider bay lists all the positions it consumes. A taller bay lists all its occupied rows. Those fields prevent the same physical space from being assigned twice when a population is assembled from different module types.

Consider the Type D example. A long Type D bay in the leftmost location of the bottom rack unit is named Row one, Long one point two, D. The electrical requirement states five thousand amperes at forty degrees Celsius ambient and three thousand fifty meters elevation, with natural convection only. The assembly must satisfy touch-temperature requirements and remain within the specified busbar clip's temperature rating. Those conditions belong beside the capability claim.

Both the power and return conductors must be electrically continuous through the assembly height to form a single power zone. A selected power shelf may have its own output voltage and compensation behavior. The contribution identifies typical nominal outputs, but directs the implementer to the actual power-shelf specification for the detailed range. Power shelves themselves remain outside the MGX contribution's scope.

One editorial issue needs a bounded interpretation. Table three is captioned as a fourteen-hundred-ampere parasitics table inside the five-thousand-ampere section. This course does not use those parasitic numbers as an unqualified five-thousand-ampere guarantee. Applicability needs clarification.

slides.title: Return bonding and rack grounding are separate

bullets.text: Two orderable variants: isolated return or hard return-to-chassis bond.
The chassis/U-channel connects electrically to the rack at top and bottom.

slides.transcript:
The contribution permits two busbar variants with different return-bonding arrangements. One isolates chassis and return. The other provides a hard tie between return and chassis. This allows different rack grounding schemes with limited hardware changes.

That choice is distinct from grounding the busbar chassis to the rack. The chassis or U-channel must connect electrically to the rack to maintain a common ground potential. The contribution specifies connections at both the top and bottom. The mounting interfaces use masking or serrated washers to establish the electrical contact, and the relevant rack contact region is masked to minimize impedance.

Do not describe an isolated-return variant as an ungrounded chassis. Isolation concerns the return-to-chassis relationship. The separate chassis-to-rack connection still applies. Likewise, selecting a bonded-return variant does not excuse an uncontrolled rack contact surface.

During review, draw the actual relationships among positive conductor, return conductor, chassis, and rack. Identify the selected variant and the features that implement each connection. Keep a conductive spacer or grounding bolt associated with the variant it supports. Keep masked surfaces and mounting contacts associated with the chassis-to-rack path.

This distinction also affects test applicability. The manufacturing dielectric requirements include a stated exception for the hard-grounded version in the relevant conductor-to-chassis tests. We'll review that condition alongside the electrical evidence. An insulating layer and a thermal-transfer layer serve different purposes. The reference design shows G T S three four eight one five one H T S for insulation and T G P three five zero zero for the thermal layer. The latter starts at one point five millimeters and is compressed to one millimeter.

The fastening arrangement must achieve the required compression while retaining the components. It must also avoid removing copper in the high-power connection positions. A nominal layer thickness in an exploded model is therefore not the finished condition. The assembled fastening and compression evidence matters.

The thermal requirements include limits for surfaces accessible to fingers and hands. Internal conductors must remain below the relevant busbar clip temperature rating under the system's worst-case thermal conditions. Clip suitability must be evaluated for the actual system. Venting and perforation geometry have their own structural and access constraints.

The busbar power-map discussion states that cooling should keep the maximum temperature at one hundred five degrees Celsius or below. The displayed dissipation map is an example configuration, not a prediction for every rack. Do not replace a clip-specific limit or a touch limit with that example number.

The section reveal separates insulation, thermal transfer, and cooling regions so their relationships can be followed. The heat indicators explain the path schematically; they are not a measured temperature map. A useful acceptance record states the selected layers, their assembled compression, the electrical isolation evidence, and the temperatures measured at the relevant surfaces and interfaces.

The measurement includes the total send and return path. A measurement across a shorter segment or only one conductor would answer a different question.

A dielectric withstand test, often called high-pot, evaluates the electrical insulation under an applied test voltage. The manufacturing requirement applies to one hundred percent of busbar assemblies. It specifies a minimum of one point two kilovolts, a ten-second ramp, a thirty-second hold, and maximum leakage of ten microamperes.

Read the tested pairs and the exception. Power-to-return is identified separately from power-to-chassis and return-to-chassis. The latter conductor-to-chassis statement is not applicable to the hard-grounded version. Record the actual grounding variant when interpreting the test evidence.

The reliability requirement includes fifty mating and unmating cycles with the specified connector without wearing out the plating. Units also carry part number and revision, date code, and a high-pot stamp. Those records connect a manufactured unit to the reviewed configuration.

The exercise is to compare the evidence for isolated-return and bonded-return variants. Identify which test-applicability statement changes, and preserve the configuration alongside the results. This is a requirement interpretation, not a live test procedure.

The rack table uses different burst wording. Preserve each table's wording and boundary until that editorial difference is clarified; don't silently merge them into one new test rule.

Read the fitting arrangement with the actual geometry. The reference assumes a brazed or soldered right-angle connection, and requires the structural treatment around the enclosure cutout. The selection must account for the protruding fitting's reliability and robustness.

For review, follow the complete path from the manifold through the quick disconnect, hose, fitting, and cold plate. Attach the selected fluid, temperature, pressure, and flow conditions to that path. A component label or a nominal C A D connection cannot establish hydraulic or joint performance on its own.

slides.title: Follow the heat to the power-shelf contact

figure.alt: Attributed source views of the liquid-cooled DC/DC shelf rear interfaces and busbar-clip cutaway. TBD input and management labels are retained.

TBD input and management labels are retained.

Liquid cooling the power supply does not automatically establish the temperature at its electrical contact. In Huntington's Summit example, removing shelf airflow removes a cooling path that had helped the busbar clip. Contact resistance still produces heat at the interface. The design therefore adds liquid cooling at that contact region.

The shelf view shows the electrical input, the output connection, management ports, and liquid couplings. The proposed one-rack-unit supply and the higher-level redundancy arrangement are design choices for this implementation. The electrical blind-mate connection enables the selected service approach. Keep it separate from the liquid connector and floating mechanism already introduced. They perform different jobs and need their own compatibility evidence.

The cutaway is labeled as a two-thousand-thirty-six-ampere clip. That is a component example. It does not replace the MGX busbar assembly's five-thousand-ampere requirement. Some input and management labels remain marked to be determined; the drawing is not a released interface-control specification.

For an integration review, identify the installed supply, electrical contact, cooling path, and actual load. Ask for temperature evidence at the contact as well as the surrounding assembly. A move toward fully liquid-cooled supplies also does not change the distinct tray and rack heat-capture boundaries in MGX version one point two. Follow the heat, and keep each claim attached to the component and boundary it describes.

slides.title: Float accommodates a controlled misalignment

figure.alt: Source sectional views and controlled schematic motion showing gathering, float, nominal overmate, and overdrive.
figure.caption: Nominal 0.5 mm overmate and 3 mm allowed overdrive are different states. Spring-load figures are estimated source values.

entries.text: Source sectional views explain permitted movement. Expanded display states are not a verified actuation model.

text_inventory.review_record: Final native images / encoded states and transition frames visually reviewed; OCR used as transcription assistance.

slides.transcript:
A blind-mate connection must gather and engage despite the permitted misalignment of the complete system. The tray-side mechanism captures the UQD insert on a hose adaptor between washers with a preloaded spring. This supports simultaneous radial and rotational motion. On the rack side, the socket and lead-in cap improve gathering at the manifold connection.

Float is the controlled movement provided to accommodate that misalignment. It complements the rack, support, rail, and tray references; it does not remove the need to align those features. The assembled interface still needs the correct location and engagement state.

The source sectional views distinguish nominal overmate from allowed overdrive. Figure seventy-four identifies a nominal position at zero point five millimeters overmate and shows three millimeters allowed overdrive. They are not two descriptions of the same position.

Figure seventy-five labels an initial preload of fifty-five pounds and an estimated eighty-two pounds at the illustrated three-millimeter overdrive state. These are the source's spring-loading illustrations. Do not treat the estimated spring load as a universal total tray insertion force; a complete engagement can also include interconnect and busbar contributions.

The teaching sequence expands the motion for visibility. It shows approach, gathering, the role of permitted float, and the indicated axial states. It is a source-based explanation, not a verified actuation model. For the exercise, annotate the nominal and overdrive positions, then identify which rack and tray references must remain controlled for the mechanism to function as intended.

slides.title: Read Table 9 at the rack and node boundaries

bullets.text: UQD locations are defined in Figures 76–77.
Rack flow target: up to 350 LPM; maximum dissipation: 250 kW.
Node differential pressure: ~10 psid at target flow with one mated UQD pair.

figure.caption: Position references and hydraulic requirements answer different parts of the same interface review.

slides.transcript:
The tray-side universal quick disconnect positions are specified in Figures seventy-six and seventy-seven. Read their references from the one-rack-unit chassis and connect them to the rack manifold arrangement. A hydraulic requirement does not replace this dimensional alignment check.

Rack Table nine states a target sustained flow up to three hundred fifty liters per minute and maximum rack power dissipation of two hundred fifty kilowatts. It lists an eighty-five-percent rack liquid heat-capture ratio. Those values describe the indicated rack requirements, not the smaller busbar loop in Table four.

The differential-pressure entry is approximately ten pounds per square inch differential for a node at target flow, with one mated universal quick-disconnect pair. Preserve that node and connection boundary. Do not present it as the pressure drop of every component or the entire rack loop.

Maximum operating pressure is five bar gauge, also shown as seventy-two pounds per square inch gauge. Minimum burst pressure is fifteen bar gauge, or two hundred seventeen pounds per square inch gauge. Filtration is listed as twenty-five micrometers and fifty micrometers. The table does not provide a complete filter-placement design.

For a review exercise, separate the busbar, node, tray, and rack rows into their actual boundaries. Record the selected operating condition and connection configuration beside each requirement. Then identify the evidence needed for the proposed loop. A useful review avoids combining a dimension, a flow target, and a pressure value that belong to different interfaces without saying so.

slides.title: Review the joint, the spill path, and the wetted material

bullets.text: Base pan, rearward overflow away from IT, and leak sensor are specified.
Check hose/barb/clamp compatibility at the required temperature and pressure.
Peroxide-cured EPDM is required for hoses in the wetted-material list.
Structural aluminum and wetted aluminum have different applicability.

figure.alt: Schematic review showing fluid joint, containment, sensor, and wetted-material categories.
figure.caption: The spill-path illustration is schematic. Material compatibility applies to the actual wetted surfaces and fluid.

entries.text: Actual fluid + exposed metals, seals, hose, sealants, and lubricants

text_inventory.review_record: Final native images / encoded states and transition frames visually reviewed; OCR used as transcription assistance.

slides.transcript:
Liquid integrity includes the joint, the response to a leak, and the material exposed to the fluid. The busbar requires a base pan for containment. If it overflows, fluid should be directed toward the rack rear and away from the information technology equipment.

A leakage sensor is also required; its location and mechanism depend on the design. The hose joint needs its own compatibility review. Barbs must meet the selected hose specification under the required temperature and pressure conditions. Ear clamps are recommended with supplier-appropriate sizing and application.

The contribution states that worm-gear clamps should not be used. A clampless hose option needs supplier confirmation of geometry and testing. Preserve those differences in requirement strength. The wetted-material list identifies approved material families and an avoid list.

It requires peroxide-cured E P D M for hoses. Some lubricant alternatives depend on compatibility testing. The review therefore needs the actual fluid and actual exposed materials, not just a generic family name.

Aluminum on the wetted-material avoid list does not mean that every structural or chassis part must be aluminum free. Applicability depends on whether the material contacts the fluid.

The printed brass-composition wording is ambiguous, so this course does not turn it into a precise zinc-content limit. During acceptance, identify the joint and its qualification conditions, the containment and detection implementation, and the exposed materials. Keep compatibility records tied to that configuration.

A nominal fluid path is not proof that its seals, hose, fitting, and materials remain suitable over the required operating conditions.

slides.title: Keep location, engagement state, and fluid boundary together
items: UQD, fanless-bay MQD, and busbar MQD locations are distinct.
Table 4 and Table 9 describe different boundaries.
Float complements the controlled alignment chain.
Nominal overmate, overdrive, and estimated spring loading are different facts.
Acceptance includes joint, containment, detection, and wetted-material evidence.
slides.transcript:
The liquid review starts with the interface location. Rack and tray, fanless bay, and busbar connections use different specified arrangements. Attach the connector family and revision to its actual place in the system.

Keep the thermal and hydraulic boundaries separate. The fanless tray's cooling measure, the busbar loop conditions, the node differential pressure, and the rack heat-capture requirement answer different questions.

The floating mechanism supports gathering and engagement within a controlled alignment system. Nominal overmate and allowed overdrive describe different states, and the estimated spring loading does not represent every force in a complete tray engagement.

Finally, review the hose joint, spill path, sensor, and actual wetted materials. Compatibility evidence belongs to the selected fluid and exposed configuration. You should now be able to annotate an engagement state and separate busbar conditions from rack requirements in a source-linked cooling review.

slides.transcript: Module six. Load cases, qualification, and integration review. We'll connect the interface geometry to the documented connector-force cases and the evidence needed to accept a complete implementation. We'll distinguish illustrative arithmetic from structural validation, compare the twenty-seven and thirty-six-rack-unit examples, and separate manufacturing checks from rack-level thermal and transport qualification. The final exercise builds a review record with source requirements, explicit assumptions, and the evidence still needed.

slides.title: Connect the interface design to acceptance evidence
slides.subtitle: By the end of this module, you will be able to:
objectives: Read the documented mating/unmating cases with consistent units.
State assumptions behind a derived connector-force budget.
Allocate manufacturing, thermal, transport, and compliance evidence.
Complete a source-linked acceptance review for a proposed configuration.
slides.transcript:
By the end of this module, you'll be able to interpret a connector-force diagram as a defined example case. You'll identify the tray type, mating or unmating condition, and the source units before performing arithmetic. You'll state any assumption that the listed forces act together.

You'll then connect the force locations to the mounting and reinforcement geometry. A calculated subtotal is useful, but it does not establish a support rating or a measured insertion force.

You'll also separate the evidence collected by manufacturing from the rack-level thermal, transport, and integration review. Finally, you'll assess a proposed fanless module, bay population, cartridge, grounding variant, and cooling boundary. The acceptance matrix records the requirement, source, implementation assumption, evidence, and unresolved item. That record turns a collection of familiar components into a reviewable engineering claim.

slides.title: Add one defined case, then inspect the load path

figure.alt: 27RU switch maximum-mating example with staged force contributions and a derived illustrative subtotal.
figure.caption: Derived 595.7 lb subtotal assumes all listed maximum mating contributions act together. It is not a support rating or measured insertion force.

entries.text: Illustrative simultaneous maxima. Derived arithmetic is separate from measured force and structural qualification.

text_inventory.review_record: Final native images / encoded states and transition frames visually reviewed; OCR used as transcription assistance.

slides.transcript:
A force budget needs one defined case. The twenty-seven-rack-unit source drawings distinguish switch and compute trays, and mating from unmating. The force tables are labeled in pounds. Keep that case identity and unit attached to every value you use.

Take the switch maximum-mating row in Figure eighty-one as an illustrative exercise. It lists two universal quick-disconnect contributions of eighty-two pounds each, four interconnect contributions of one hundred two point three pounds each, and a busbar contribution of twenty-two point five pounds.

If all those listed maxima are assumed to act together, the quick-disconnect subtotal is one hundred sixty-four pounds. The interconnect subtotal is four hundred nine point two. Adding the busbar contribution produces five hundred ninety-five point seven pounds. This is derived arithmetic under an explicitly stated simultaneous-loading assumption.

It is not a measured tray insertion force, a frame capacity, or proof that a particular support arrangement is adequate. Real engagement depends on the chosen interfaces, their states and sequence, the assembly, and any additional forces relevant to that implementation.

The source support details show alignment and mounting features around the cartridge, including the top and bottom positioning arrangements and reinforcement structure. Trace the force locations into those supports. Then identify the structural evidence needed for the actual configuration.

The review separates two conclusions: what a defined example's listed contributions add to under your assumption, and what the manufactured system has demonstrated. Keep both conclusions visible so illustrative arithmetic cannot be mistaken for validation.

slides.title: The 36RU examples change both case and units

bullets.text: 27RU source diagrams use lb; 36RU diagrams use N.
Switch and compute connector contributions differ.
Support geometry, connector population, and assumptions remain case specific.

figure.alt: Source 27RU compute and 36RU switch/compute force diagrams with their original unit labels.
figure.caption: Subtotals are derived from each source maximum-mating row under the same illustrative simultaneous-loading assumption.

text_inventory.review_record: Final native images / encoded states and transition frames visually reviewed; OCR used as transcription assistance.

slides.transcript:
The thirty-six-rack-unit examples use newtons, while the twenty-seven-rack-unit diagrams use pounds. A comparison must preserve both the unit and the example. Converting units alone does not make two connector populations or support arrangements equivalent.

The switch maximum-mating row in Figure eighty-three lists two quick-disconnect contributions of three hundred sixty-five newtons, four interconnect contributions of ninety newtons, and one busbar contribution of one hundred newtons. Under the same illustrative simultaneous-loading assumption, the subtotal is one thousand one hundred ninety newtons.

The thirty-six-rack-unit compute case in Figure eighty-four uses nineteen newtons for each of the four interconnect contributions. With the same listed quick-disconnect and busbar maxima, its derived subtotal is nine hundred six newtons. The difference follows from the documented case, not just the cartridge height.

The twenty-seven-rack-unit compute maximum row likewise differs from its switch row. Its corresponding derived subtotal is four hundred thirty-three point seven pounds. All four subtotals remain illustrative arithmetic, with the same stated assumption about the listed maxima acting together.

Review the actual mounting and alignment drawings with each case. A changed connector, guide, bracket, cartridge height, or support spacing may change which evidence applies. Don't select a lower subtotal from one case and a structural conclusion from another without justification.

The engineering record should identify the source case, units, interface population, loading assumption, and implementation-specific support evidence. That creates a traceable comparison instead of a table of apparently interchangeable numbers.

slides.title: Thermal steady state and transport answer different questions

bullets.text: Full rack at maximum load; allow thermal steady state.
Measure the outer touch hotspot and internal clip-region hotspot.
Packaged L11 vibration, drop, impact, and handling have their own requirements.

figure.alt: Schematic test-boundary comparison separating operating thermal measurements from packaged rack transport tests.
figure.caption: Test setup and acceptance conditions must match the claim being evaluated.

entries.text: Separate the tested configuration, condition, location, and acceptance limit.

text_inventory.review_record: Final native images / encoded states and transition frames visually reviewed; OCR used as transcription assistance.

slides.transcript:
A rack-level thermal test and a packaged transport test establish different kinds of evidence. Keep their setups and acceptance conditions separate.

Transient input-power behavior is another boundary. Huntington's Summit example uses capacitor energy and intelligent power smoothing to shape the input seen by the A C supply. Its on-and-off plot illustrates that implementation under the shown conditions. It does not replace steady-state temperature testing or establish identical performance for every workload.

During rack integration, the contribution calls for a full rack operating at maximum load, with enough time to reach thermal steady state. Thermocouples are placed on the outer surface at the maximum touch-temperature hotspot and internally near the hottest busbar clip region. Those locations address different temperature limits. A measurement at a convenient cool surface would not answer either question reliably.

The packaged L eleven requirements address rack-and-roll deployment, with the option for liquid-charged systems. The listed vibration requirement includes two hours at one to two hundred hertz and zero point five four G R M S, with no top load. Another two-hour air-vibration requirement references the stated A S T M method.

The contribution also lists a six-inch rotational-drop condition, four incline impacts at four feet per second, and a twenty-two-degree tip test in each direction. The detailed methods must be read with the referenced documents and the actual packaged implementation. This course identifies the required evidence; it does not provide a lifting or live-test procedure.

For acceptance, identify which configuration was tested, how it was instrumented or packaged, and which source conditions were evaluated. Separate operating temperature, shipment conditions, and handling claims. A common rack family or an earlier test report is useful only when its configuration and conditions apply to the system being accepted.

slides.subtitle: A report must identify configuration, conditions, results, and applicability.
rows: Maximum-load thermal results; configured load/support evidence
Actual fluid/wetted materials; applicable referenced compliance records
Drawing/revision, variant, assumptions, and open items
slides.transcript:
Qualification becomes more useful when each requirement has an owner and an acceptance condition. The contribution requires suppliers to conduct a comprehensive test plan to ensure specifications and reliability over the product lifetime, and calls for a full report for evaluation and approval. The listed minimum busbar tests support that broader responsibility; they are not a complete substitute for it.

Manufacturing evidence applies to actual assemblies. It includes the specified liquid and electrical checks, appropriate tested conductor pairs, and traceability labels. Keep the grounding variant and unit revision linked to the results.

Rack integration evidence covers the completed configuration. It includes maximum-load thermal behavior and the support or loading evidence for the actual interface arrangement. A component report may support this review, but it does not automatically establish the assembled rack's performance.

Material and safety evidence also needs the correct scope. Review the actual coolant and wetted surfaces, the required fluid documentation, and the compliance requirements referenced by this contribution. The course preserves the standards and editions at their recorded scope. A deployment's certification review must establish the requirements applicable to its actual product and jurisdiction.

An acceptance matrix should therefore identify the requirement, source page or drawing, configuration, evidence owner, test conditions, result, and unresolved item. If the implementation changes, reassess applicability rather than merely retaining the old passed stamp.

This structure helps distinguish missing evidence from a genuine requirement failure. It also makes open assumptions visible before an engineering claim is accepted.

Use the final exercise to assemble the interface review into one acceptance record. The scenario proposes a full-size fanless host processor module with Type B and Type E bays, a twenty-seven-rack-unit compute cartridge case, an isolated-return busbar, and the applicable busbar and rack cooling boundaries. These are scenario assumptions, not a declared validated product.

For a power-rack implementation, also identify the voltage domain and connector rating at each conversion boundary. Record the selected redundancy configuration and which cooling boundary the evidence covers. Use the Summit design as context; use the applicable component specification and test report to support the acceptance claim.

The review packet supplies a nominal C A D fit. Identify the controlling dimensions, datum chain, tolerances, retention interfaces, and selected support evidence needed to move beyond that fit. Use the correct compute load case; don't import the switch subtotal merely because the cartridge height is the same.

A partial voltage-drop result is also supplied. Ask whether it follows the specified top-source and bottom-loopback arrangement and includes both send and return at the rated current. Then identify the applicable manufacturing dielectric evidence for the isolated-return variant.

The liquid connection locations are shown, but the packet leaves joint qualification, the containment and sensor implementation, and the actual wetted-material compatibility open. Separate Table four busbar conditions from Table nine rack requirements when requesting those records.

For each acceptance claim, record the requirement and source, the proposed configuration, any assumption, the evidence owner, and the unresolved item. The downloadable worksheet provides the same review structure.

The exercise's goal is not to declare every familiar component acceptable. It is to explain which claims are supported, which need more evidence, and which source condition or interface boundary governs the decision.
